extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of English literature / readers of Ben Jonson's Volpone
extracted.subtask_description: A Gutenberg edition page containing a biographical/critical introduction to Ben Jonson and the beginning of his play Volpone: dedication, prologue, dramatis personae, argument, and opening of Act I. Useful for readers studying the play and Jonson's aesthetic precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral character of the poet
rubrics_metrics.description: “the impossibility of any man's being the good poet, without first being a good man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jonson argues that a true poet must be morally sound; poetry's authority and capacity to instruct depend on the poet's virtue. The poet should be a teacher of manners and virtues, not merely a clever rhymer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of poetry — mix profit with pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: “to mix profit with your pleasure; ... the doctrine, which is the principal end of poesie, to inform men in the best reason of living.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama and poetry should both delight and instruct: entertain the audience while imparting moral or practical lessons — 'profit' (instruction) combined with 'pleasure' (entertainment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ribaldry, profanation, and blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson censures “ribaldry, profanation, blasphemy, all license of offence to God and man” and states he has “ever trembled to think toward the least profaneness; have loathed the use of such foul and unwashed bawdry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from obscene, profane, or blasphemous language and bawdy material that degrades the dignity of poetry and the stage; maintain decorum and moral restraint in subject and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the laws of time, place, and persons (classical unities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologue: “The laws of time, place, persons he observeth, From no needful rule he swerveth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect classical dramatic conventions (unity of time, place, and person) and other necessary formal rules of stagecraft unless deviation is purposefully justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes and comic material should fit the fable (originality and integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologue: “Nor made he his play for jests stolen from each table, but makes jests to fit his fable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic elements should arise organically from the plot and characters rather than being unrelated or popular 'table-jests' borrowed for cheap effect; favour originality and integration with the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid low farce and gratuitous physical buffoonery
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologue: “no eggs are broken, Nor quaking custards with fierce teeth affrighted ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from gross slapstick or spectacle used solely for cheap laughs; prefer refined comedy that elicits laughter without resorting to vulgar physical gimmicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in satirical bitterness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologue: “All gall and copperas from his ink he draineth, Only a little salt remaineth...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be sharp but tempered — retain wit and edge without overwhelming bitterness; use restraint so the work remains pleasurable as well as corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and literary finish; avoid rhapsody
rubrics_metrics.description: “His theory demanded design and the perfection of literary finish. He was furthest from the rhapsodist and the careless singer of an idle day.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for careful composition, structural design, and polished phrasing; avoid loose, formless, or overly improvisatory writing. Economy of language is prized (e.g., “not a word too much”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance rhetorical finish with spontaneity in lyric poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: On Jonson's lyrics: while “beautiful in form, deft and graceful,” they sometimes show “a certain stiffness and formality,” and “epigram and occasional verse where rhetorical finish and pointed wit less interfere with the spontaneity and emotion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In shorter lyric forms, preserve spontaneity and feeling; do not let excessive rhetorical polish deaden natural emotion. Match finish to the emotional demands of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned use of sources: convert and improve upon predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's authorship involved “an ability ... to convert the substance or riches of another poet to his own use.” He read classics and contemporary Latin writings and sometimes translated or adapted passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground work in broad learning and classical models; borrow where useful but transform and better the source material so the result is original and sovereign, not mere plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic poet's duties: imitate justice and stir gentle affections
rubrics_metrics.description: “it being the office of a comic poet to imitate justice, and instruct to life, as well as purity of language, or stir up gentle affections.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should model moral order (punish vice, reward virtue as appropriate), instruct audiences about life, maintain purity of language, and evoke mild, humane emotions rather than coarse hatred or vindictiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism and lifelike distinctness in characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic praises Jonson: “the personages stand out with such lifelike distinctness in their several kinds, and the whole is animated with such verve and resourcefulness...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be drawn from observed life with recognizable types and convincing detail; even caricature should be grounded in realism and human truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for ease, propriety, innocence, and doctrine when revising plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson says he laboured to “reduce not only the ancient forms, but manners of the scene, the easiness, the propriety, the innocence, and last, the doctrine,” when revising for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising dramatic work, prioritize naturalness (ease), appropriateness of style (propriety), moral cleanliness (innocence), and clear instructive purpose (doctrine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal lampoon; target vice not private reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson defends himself: “where have I been particular? where personal? except to a mimic, cheater, bawd, or buffoon...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should generally attack types and vices rather than single living persons' private reputations; personal, spiteful lampooning is to be avoided except when the target is manifestly deserving (public scoundrels).
